<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{sim}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})=\mathbf{x}^{\top}\mathbf{y}/\|\mathbf{x}\|\|\mathbf{y}\|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mtext>sim</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐱</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝐲</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>𝐱</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐲</mi></mrow><mo>/</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mi>𝐱</mi><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mi>𝐲</mi><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{sim}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})=\mathbf{x}^{\top}\mathbf{y}/\|\mathbf{x}\|\|\mathbf{y}\|</annotation></semantics></math> is cosine similarity. Above, <math id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Z_{i}^{\text{P}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>Z</mi><mi>i</mi><mtext>P</mtext></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Z_{i}^{\text{P}}</annotation></semantics></math> corresponds to the positive, <math id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Z_{i}^{\text{HN}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>Z</mi><mi>i</mi><mtext>HN</mtext></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Z_{i}^{\text{HN}}</annotation></semantics></math> corresponds to the hard negatives, <math id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Z_{i}^{\text{IB}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>Z</mi><mi>i</mi><mtext>IB</mtext></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Z_{i}^{\text{IB}}</annotation></semantics></math> corresponds to in-batch negatives, and <math id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Z_{i}^{\text{STN}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>Z</mi><mi>i</mi><mtext>STN</mtext></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Z_{i}^{\text{STN}}</annotation></semantics></math> corresponds to same-tower negatives <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">20</a>]</cite>. <math id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{1}_{\text{TN}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mn>𝟙</mn><mtext>TN</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{1}_{\text{TN}}</annotation></semantics></math> masks out false negatives from duplicates:</p>
<table id="S2.EGx1" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S2.E3"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S2.E3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\mathbb{1}_{\text{TN}}(i,j)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mn>𝟙</mn><mtext>TN</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\mathbb{1}_{\text{TN}}(i,j)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S2.E3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=\begin{cases}0&amp;\text{if }\mathbf{q}_{i}=\mathbf{q}_{j}\text{ or }\mathbf{p}_{i}^{+}=\mathbf{p}_{j}^{+},\\
1&amp;\text{otherwise,}\end{cases}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>{</mo><mtable columnspacing="5pt" rowspacing="0pt"><mtr><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mn>0</mn></mtd><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mrow><mrow><mtext>if </mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝐪</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐪</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext> or </mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐩</mi><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo></msubsup></mrow><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐩</mi><mi>j</mi><mo>+</mo></msubsup></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mn>1</mn></mtd><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mtext>otherwise,</mtext></mtd></mtr></mtable></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=\begin{cases}0&amp;\text{if }\mathbf{q}_{i}=\mathbf{q}_{j}\text{ or }\mathbf{p}_{i}^{+}=\mathbf{p}_{j}^{+},\\
1&amp;\text{otherwise,}\end{cases}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(3)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We forego the hardness weighting mechanism from our previous model as it amplifies noisy or weakly associated positive pairs, especially during early training, and compounds gradient scale imbalances between tasks of different modalities. We add same-tower negatives to prevent queries and targets from clustering into disjoint subspaces.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">For listwise ranking data with <math id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>P</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P</annotation></semantics></math> ordered positives <math id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\mathbf{p}_{i,1}^{+}\succ\dots\succ\mathbf{p}_{i,P}^{+})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐩</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>+</mo></msubsup><mo>≻</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">⋯</mi><mo>≻</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐩</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo></msubsup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\mathbf{p}_{i,1}^{+}\succ\dots\succ\mathbf{p}_{i,P}^{+})</annotation></semantics></math> per query, we train both on extracted triplets using <math id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{C}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mi>C</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{C}</annotation></semantics></math> and on the full ranked lists using a listwise loss that extends <math id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{C}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mi>C</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{C}</annotation></semantics></math> based on the Plackett–Luce model, as in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xia et al. [21]</a></cite>:</p>
<table id="S2.E4" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_table">
<tbody>
<tr id="S2.E4X" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S2.E4X.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{C}^{\text{list}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mi>C</mi><mtext>list</mtext></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{C}^{\text{list}}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S2.E4X.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{BP}\sum_{i=1}^{B}\sum_{r=1}^{P}\log\frac{Z_{i,r}^{\text{P}}}{\sum_{k=r}^{P}Z_{i,k}^{\text{P}}+Z_{i}^{\text{HN}}+Z_{i}^{\text{IB}}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo rspace="0em">=</mo><mo lspace="0em">−</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo></mstyle><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><msup><mrow></mrow><mi>B</mi></msup><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo></mstyle><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><msup><mrow></mrow><mi>P</mi></msup><mi>log</mi><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><msubsup><mi>Z</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow><mtext>P</mtext></msubsup><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow><mi>P</mi></msubsup><msubsup><mi>Z</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow><mtext>P</mtext></msubsup></mrow><mo>+</mo><msubsup><mi>Z</mi><mi>i</mi><mtext>HN</mtext></msubsup><mo>+</mo><msubsup><mi>Z</mi><mi>i</mi><mtext>IB</mtext></msubsup></mrow></mfrac></mstyle></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{BP}\sum_{i=1}^{B}\sum_{r=1}^{P}\log\frac{Z_{i,r}^{\text{P}}}{\sum_{k=r}^{P}Z_{i,k}^{\text{P}}+Z_{i}^{\text{HN}}+Z_{i}^{\text{IB}}}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="2" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equationgroup ltx_align_right">(4)</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S2.E4Xa" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S2.E4Xa.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle Z_{i,r}^{\text{P}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>Z</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow><mtext>P</mtext></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle Z_{i,r}^{\text{P}}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S2.E4Xa.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=e^{\text{sim}(\mathbf{q}_{i},\mathbf{p}_{i,r}^{+})/\tau},\qquad Z_{i}^{\text{IB}}=\sum_{j=1}^{B}\mathbb{1}_{\text{TN}}(i,j)\Bigl(\sum_{k=1}^{P}e^{\text{sim}(\mathbf{q}_{i},\mathbf{p}_{j,k}^{+})/\tau}+\sum_{\mathbf{p}_{j}^{-}}e^{\text{sim}(\mathbf{q}_{i},\mathbf{p}_{j}^{-})/\tau}\Bigr)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mrow><mtext>sim</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐪</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐩</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>/</mo><mi>τ</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><mo rspace="2.167em">,</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>Z</mi><mi>i</mi><mtext>IB</mtext></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>B</mi></munderover></mstyle><mrow><msub><mn>𝟙</mn><mtext>TN</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo mathsize="1.600em">,</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.600em" minsize="1.600em">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>P</mi></munderover></mstyle><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mrow><mtext>sim</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐪</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐩</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>/</mo><mi>τ</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><munder><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐩</mi><mi>j</mi><mo>−</mo></msubsup></munder></mstyle><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mrow><mtext>sim</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐪</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐩</mi><mi>j</mi><mo>−</mo></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>/</mo><mi>τ</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow><mo maxsize="1.600em" minsize="1.600em">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=e^{\text{sim}(\mathbf{q}_{i},\mathbf{p}_{i,r}^{+})/\tau},\qquad Z_{i}^{\text{IB}}=\sum_{j=1}^{B}\mathbb{1}_{\text{TN}}(i,j)\Bigl(\sum_{k=1}^{P}e^{\text{sim}(\mathbf{q}_{i},\mathbf{p}_{j,k}^{+})/\tau}+\sum_{\mathbf{p}_{j}^{-}}e^{\text{sim}(\mathbf{q}_{i},\mathbf{p}_{j}^{-})/\tau}\Bigr)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p3.2" class="ltx_p">Here, we contrast each rank-<math id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math> positive against all lower-ranked positives (<math id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k&gt;r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k&gt;r</annotation></semantics></math>) in addition to hard and in-batch negatives, with <math id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{1}_{\text{TN}}(i,j)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mn>𝟙</mn><mtext>TN</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{1}_{\text{TN}}(i,j)</annotation></semantics></math> adapted to mask out in-batch negatives that duplicate <math id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{p}_{i,r}^{+}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>𝐩</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{p}_{i,r}^{+}</annotation></semantics></math>. We also add small squared-hinge penalties on positive and hard-negative similarities to calibrate the absolute score distribution for threshold-based tasks.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Spread-out regularizer</h4>

<div id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The second loss is based on the global orthogonal regularizer (GOR) introduced in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al. [22]</a></cite>. The idea is to make the embeddings of a random pair of inputs have similar statistical properties (mean and second moment) as two points independently and uniformly sampled from the unit sphere. Following EmbeddingGemma 1 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">23</a>]</cite>, we use only the “second moment” term of the regularizer’s original definition, as we find this also sufficiently pushes the “mean” term towards its target value:</p>
<table id="S2.EGx2" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S2.E5"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S2.E5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{S}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mi>S</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{S}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S2.E5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=\frac{1}{B\,(B-1)}\sum_{1\leq i\neq j\leq B}(\mathbf{q}_{i}^{\top}\mathbf{q}_{j})^{2}+\,\frac{1}{B\,(B-1)}\sum_{1\leq i\neq j\leq B}(\mathbf{p}_{i}^{+\top}\mathbf{p}_{j}^{+})^{2}." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo lspace="0.170em">⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><munder><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>≤</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>≠</mo><mi>j</mi><mo>≤</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow></munder></mstyle><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐪</mi><mi>i</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝐪</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.392em">+</mo><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo lspace="0.170em">⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><munder><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>≤</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>≠</mo><mi>j</mi><mo>≤</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow></munder></mstyle><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐩</mi><mi>i</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo><mo lspace="0em">⁣</mo><mo>⊤</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐩</mi><mi>j</mi><mo>+</mo></msubsup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=\frac{1}{B\,(B-1)}\sum_{1\leq i\neq j\leq B}(\mathbf{q}_{i}^{\top}\mathbf{q}_{j})^{2}+\,\frac{1}{B\,(B-1)}\sum_{1\leq i\neq j\leq B}(\mathbf{p}_{i}^{+\top}\mathbf{p}_{j}^{+})^{2}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(5)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">This loss encourages the model to produce embeddings that are spread out over the embedding space, to fully utilize its expressive power. Embedding spaces have been observed to form narrow cones <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">24</a>, <a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">25</a>, <a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">26</a>, <a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">27</a>]</cite>, but there are theoretical and empirical benefits to isotropy <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">28</a>, <a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">29</a>]</cite>, including performance in downstream tasks. Note that pushing random pairs toward orthogonality complements the squared-hinge penalties above to make scores more calibrated and interpretable. Enforcing isotropy also aims to ensure that a) the model is robust to weight and embedding quantization, and b) the embeddings can be retrieved efficiently in vector databases using approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) algorithms.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Distillation loss</h4>

<div id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The final is an embedding matching loss based on <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kim et al. [30]</a></cite>. In contrast to previous distillation research which has relied only on the teacher’s query-document relevance scores as a signal <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">31</a>, <a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">32</a>]</cite>, this loss directly aligns EmbeddingGemma 2’s embedding space with that of a teacher model, allowing it to more effectively learn from the larger, more powerful Gemini Embedding 2 model. Unlike <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kim et al. [30]</a></cite>, which applies a projection layer to distill from a model with different dimensionality, we instead make use of Gemini Embedding 2’s support for lower dimensions and simply truncate the teacher embeddings. As in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schechter Vera et al. [23]</a></cite>, we apply embedding matching not only to queries and targets but also to hard negative targets, which intuitively serves to transfer the teacher’s ability to discriminate between queries and their hard negatives, and empirically does improve performance. We weigh these individual losses uniformly, letting</p>
<table id="S2.EGx3" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S2.E6"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S2.E6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{D}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mi>D</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{D}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S2.E6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=\mathcal{L}_{D}^{\mathbf{q}}+\mathcal{L}_{D}^{\mathbf{p}^{+}}+\mathcal{L}_{D}^{\mathbf{p}^{-}},\quad\text{where}\quad\mathcal{L}_{D}^{\mathbf{u}}=\frac{1}{B}\sum_{i=1}^{B}\bigl\|\mathbf{u}_{i}-\tilde{\mathbf{u}}_{i}\bigr\|_{2}^{2}\quad\text{for }\mathbf{u}\in\{\mathbf{q},\mathbf{p}^{+},\mathbf{p}^{-}\}," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mi>D</mi><mi>𝐪</mi></msubsup><mo>+</mo><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mi>D</mi><msup><mi>𝐩</mi><mo>+</mo></msup></msubsup><mo>+</mo><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mi>D</mi><msup><mi>𝐩</mi><mo>−</mo></msup></msubsup></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mtext>where</mtext><mspace style="width:1em;" width="1em"></mspace><mrow><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mi>D</mi><mi>𝐮</mi></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>B</mi></mfrac></mstyle><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>B</mi></munderover></mstyle><msubsup><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em" stretchy="true">‖</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐮</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐮</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em" stretchy="true">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow></mrow></mrow><mspace style="width:1em;" width="1em"></mspace><mrow><mrow><mtext>for </mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐮</mi></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>𝐪</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>𝐩</mi><mo>+</mo></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>𝐩</mi><mo>−</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=\mathcal{L}_{D}^{\mathbf{q}}+\mathcal{L}_{D}^{\mathbf{p}^{+}}+\mathcal{L}_{D}^{\mathbf{p}^{-}},\quad\text{where}\quad\mathcal{L}_{D}^{\mathbf{u}}=\frac{1}{B}\sum_{i=1}^{B}\bigl\|\mathbf{u}_{i}-\tilde{\mathbf{u}}_{i}\bigr\|_{2}^{2}\quad\text{for }\mathbf{u}\in\{\mathbf{q},\mathbf{p}^{+},\mathbf{p}^{-}\},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(6)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1.2" class="ltx_p">and <math id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{\mathbf{u}}_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐮</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{\mathbf{u}}_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the truncated, <math id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell_{2}</annotation></semantics></math>-normalized teacher embedding for input <math id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{u}_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐮</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{u}_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> (with <math id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{D}^{\mathbf{p}^{-}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mi>D</mi><msup><mi>𝐩</mi><mo>−</mo></msup></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{D}^{\mathbf{p}^{-}}</annotation></semantics></math> averaged over hard negatives when multiple <math id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{p}_{i}^{-}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>𝐩</mi><mi>i</mi><mo>−</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{p}_{i}^{-}</annotation></semantics></math> are present).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Matryoshka Representation Learning</h4>

<div id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We adapt the contrastive, spread-out, and distillation losses with Matryoshka Representation Learning (MRL) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">33</a>]</cite>, splitting each loss into <math id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> separate losses applied to <math id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> overlapping sub-dimensions of the embedding. EmbeddingGemma 2 provides <math id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px4.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="768" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>768</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">768</annotation></semantics></math>-dimensional embeddings, additionally supporting <math id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px4.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="512" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>512</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">512</annotation></semantics></math>-, <math id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px4.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="256" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>256</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">256</annotation></semantics></math>-, and <math id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px4.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="128" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>128</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">128</annotation></semantics></math>-dimensional embeddings via MRL.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.4 </span>Recipe</h3>

<section id="S2.SS4.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Initialization</h4>

<div id="S2.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">EmbeddingGemma 2 builds directly on Gemma 4’s extensive world knowledge and capabilities. The backbone is adapted from a pretrained Gemma 4 decoder-only model, switching the causal attention mask to bidirectional attention to enable fully contextual token representations <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">34</a>, <a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">35</a>, <a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">36</a>, <a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>]</cite>. We omit explicit adaptation stages for bidirectional attention <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">23</a>, <a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">37</a>]</cite>, which can be costly and have been shown to be unnecessary for learning expressive representations <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">23</a>, <a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">38</a>]</cite>. We also remove the PLE-specific token lookup table (detailed in <a href="#S3.T2" title="In 3.1 Per-Layer Embeddings Table ‣ 3 Ablation Studies ‣ EmbeddingGemma 2: Unified and Efficient Multimodal Representations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>), and add mean pooling <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">39</a>, <a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">23</a>]</cite>, a linear projection, and <math id="S2.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell_{2}</annotation></semantics></math>-normalization after the transformer. The vision encoder is initialized with the smaller Gemma 4 vision encoder and further trained in the two multimodal stages, which we show in <a href="#S3" title="3 Ablation Studies ‣ EmbeddingGemma 2: Unified and Efficient Multimodal Representations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> to be critical for quality. The audio encoder is bit-identical to that in the Gemma 4 E2B and E4B models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a>]</cite> and kept frozen during training.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We then train EmbeddingGemma 2 on a mixture of embedding tasks spanning various modalities and task types. In total, the model sees approximately 2.9T tokens, of which <math id="S2.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>300B are seen during text pre-finetuning, <math id="S2.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>2T during multimodal pre-finetuning, and <math id="S2.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>600B during multimodal finetuning.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS4.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Text Pre-finetuning</h4>

<div id="S2.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We begin with a pre-finetuning stage like the one in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schechter Vera et al. [23]</a></cite>. This entails a large-scale unsupervised data mixture of query-target pairs from question answering, sentence similarity, code retrieval, and web search tasks using various languages. As before, we opt for a larger batch size both to stabilize the gradient and to provide more (in-batch) negatives for each input example. In this stage we almost exclusively employ distillation loss, with only an additional contrastive loss using a small weight. Here, as with subsequent stages, tasks are sampled at pre-determined, empirically defined rates. We found the inclusion of a text-only stage important for the model’s final text quality. This stage can be seen as a form of curriculum learning, or as an implicit warm-up for the bidirectional attention, similar to <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">BehnamGhader et al. [37]</a></cite>; it has also been shown to enhance the discriminability of both text and non-text embeddings <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS4.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Multimodal Pre-finetuning</h4>

<div id="S2.SS4.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS4.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We then continue with pre-finetuning, but with a new mixture which also includes inputs with images, audio, video, and documents across unimodal, cross-modal, and mixed-modal tasks, most with additional hard negatives. The text tasks in this stage and the next include those described in the finetuning stage of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schechter Vera et al. [23]</a></cite>, which aim to cover task diversity, language diversity, and coding capability. In this stage, we exclusively employ distillation loss, to inherit the teacher’s ability to map diverse and mixed modalities into a shared semantic space. We continue training with larger batch sizes and larger learning rates, but train for twice as many steps as in text pre-finetuning to cover the expanded multimodal training set.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS4.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Multimodal Finetuning</h4>

<div id="S2.SS4.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS4.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In the finetuning stage, we completely replace distillation with contrastive loss. This allows the model to learn a tailored embedding space independent of its teacher, as the teacher’s embedding space is not optimized for the student’s architecture, size, and MRL sub-dimensions. We also add other losses which aim to shape the final embedding space to have desirable properties: spread-out regularizer and MRL losses. As in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schechter Vera et al. [23]</a></cite>, we transition to smaller learning rates and batch sizes, and shift towards higher-quality, task-specific datasets, such as tool retrieval, audio captioning, video ranking, medical imaging, visual product search, cropped-object retrieval, and academic question-answering.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS4.SSS0.Px5" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Model Merging</h4>

<div id="S2.SS4.SSS0.Px5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS4.SSS0.Px5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Finally, we combine checkpoints from our finetuning run by averaging their weights, to improve our final model’s quality and robustness. Rather than running multiple finetuning jobs, either with different data mixture rates <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">23</a>]</cite> or with different hyperparameters <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">40</a>]</cite>, we merge checkpoints along a single finetuning trajectory <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">41</a>]</cite>. Specifically, we compute an unweighted average between the final checkpoint from the finetuning run and a significantly earlier checkpoint from the same run. Like <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wortsman et al. [42]</a></cite>, which similarly merges pretrained and finetuned checkpoints, we found that this helps mitigate degradation on tasks that overfit during finetuning, while also further improving performance on tasks that already benefited from finetuning.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS4.SSS0.Px6" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Quantization-Aware Training</h4>

</span></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S2.T1.7" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 1</span>: </span><span id="S2.T1.8" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Comparison of raw and quantized EmbeddingGemma 2 and EmbeddingGemma 1 checkpoints across benchmarks covering text, vision, and audio: MTEB, MIEB(lite), and MSEB(Retrieval).
<br class="ltx_break"><sup id="S2.T1.8.1" class="ltx_sup">∗</sup>Per-block int4. <sup id="S2.T1.8.2" class="ltx_sup">†</sup>Per-channel int4. <sup id="S2.T1.8.3" class="ltx_sup">‡</sup>Different eval harnesses between float and quantized runs.
</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S2.SS4.SSS0.Px6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS4.SSS0.Px6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We additionally provide quantized versions of EmbeddingGemma 2 in different quantization configurations. We provide checkpoints with two types of weight representations for the backbone: int4 per-block (Q4_0) and int4 per-channel (Q4_C). For the modality encoders, we follow the quantization schemes used in Gemma 4: the vision encoder uses 8-bit precision for both weights and activations (W8A8), and the audio encoder uses 8-bit activation precision and {2, 4, 8}-bit weight precision varying by layer cluster.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS4.SSS0.Px6.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS4.SSS0.Px6.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We apply quantization-aware training <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">43</a>, QAT,]</cite> to both the backbone and vision encoder to minimize quality degradation (the audio encoder is taken directly from Gemma 4). However, instead of applying QAT directly in the finetuning stage as in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schechter Vera et al. [23]</a></cite>, we introduce a separate post-merging tail-patch stage in which we distill (and initialize) our QAT checkpoint from the frozen float checkpoint <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">44</a>]</cite>. This allows for a more resource-efficient QAT stage and narrows the gap in quality between the float and quantized checkpoints for some evaluations, notably MTEB(English, v2). <a href="#S2.T1" title="In Quantization-Aware Training ‣ 2.4 Recipe ‣ 2 EmbeddingGemma 2 ‣ EmbeddingGemma 2: Unified and Efficient Multimodal Representations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> shows the quality is comparable between our quantized checkpoints and our raw checkpoint (evaluated at half-precision bfloat16 weights). With Q4_C quantization, the peak on-device memory footprint during inference (including runtime compilation overhead) on a Google Pixel 11 Pro is reduced to 191 MB for text-only, 447 MB for text and vision, and 567 MB for the full multimodal model.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Ablation Studies</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We analyze some key design choices to better understand how they contributed to EmbeddingGemma 2’s ability to produce high-quality embeddings across modalities, domains, and task types. Baseline and ablation models use an intermediate recipe and so numbers are not representative of the final model. Unless otherwise stated, the experiments run finetuning on a pre-finetuned model. We evaluate the models on MMEB-v2 as it covers various tasks involving combinations of text, images, documents, and video, excluding only audio.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Per-Layer Embeddings Table</h3>

<figure id="S3.T2" class="ltx_table">

<tr id="S3.T2.3.1.3" class="ltx_tr">

<td id="S3.T2.3.1.4.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb ltx_border_r ltx_border_t">55.07</td>
<td id="S3.T2.3.1.4.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t">54.57</td>
<td id="S3.T2.3.1.4.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t">47.13</td>
<td id="S3.T2.3.1.4.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t">61.76</td></tr>
</table>
</span></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S3.T2.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 2</span>: </span><span id="S3.T2.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Results with and without a dedicated Per-Layer Embeddings (PLE) lookup table.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Gemma 3n and Gemma 4 incorporate Per-Layer Embeddings (PLE) to inject token-level information into intermediate transformer layers. Specifically, they combine a learned projection of the main token embedding with an additional dedicated PLE lookup table. However, a dedicated PLE lookup table provides no direct signals for non-text modalities and consumes additional memory.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We utilize only the projection, as described in detail in <a href="#S2.SS1" title="2.1 Architecture ‣ 2 EmbeddingGemma 2 ‣ EmbeddingGemma 2: Unified and Efficient Multimodal Representations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.1</span></a>; this way, we continue providing per-layer inputs but can omit the lookup table. We compare our approach to PLE with a lookup table in <a href="#S3.T2" title="In 3.1 Per-Layer Embeddings Table ‣ 3 Ablation Studies ‣ EmbeddingGemma 2: Unified and Efficient Multimodal Representations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>. Removing the dedicated PLE table not only reduces parameter overhead, but also strengthens performance across all three categories (notably +0.69 on Video and +0.61 on VisDoc), confirming that deriving per-layer inputs solely from the shared <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{M}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>M</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{M}</annotation></semantics></math>-dimensional embedding space improves multimodal representation quality. We also found similar improvements in text-only evaluations, where one might expect the lookup table to help the most.</p>
</div>
</section>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S3.T3.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 3</span>: </span><span id="S3.T3.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Results of continued distillation versus adding a finetuning stage with contrastive learning.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We investigate whether the gains from our finetuning stage are truly driven by a difference in recipe or merely by extending training. Starting from the multimodal pre-finetuning checkpoint, we compare running the multimodal finetuning stage against continuing distillation for an approximately compute-equivalent duration (the same number of steps, but with larger batch sizes on distillation). <a href="#S3.T3" title="In 3.2 Finetuning Stage ‣ 3 Ablation Studies ‣ EmbeddingGemma 2: Unified and Efficient Multimodal Representations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> shows that while distillation plateaus, transitioning to the finetuning recipe with contrastive and spread-out objectives boosts performance significantly for image and video tasks while yielding similar results for visual documents. This demonstrates that the finetuning stage enables the model to move beyond imitating its teacher and learn a better-optimized representation space.</p>
</div>
</section>

</span></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S3.T4.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 4</span>: </span><span id="S3.T4.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Results with trainable and frozen vision encoder.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">MLLMs often keep modality encoders frozen throughout training <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">45</a>, <a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">46</a>, <a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">47</a>, <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a>]</cite>. This strategy is also popular in recent multimodal embedding models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">48</a>, <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">9</a>, <a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">49</a>, <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a>]</cite>. For MLLMs, ablations investigating whether freezing or unfreezing the vision encoder is better are mixed <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">50</a>, <a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">45</a>, <a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">51</a>]</cite>. However, we show in <a href="#S3.T4" title="In 3.3 Vision Encoder Training ‣ 3 Ablation Studies ‣ EmbeddingGemma 2: Unified and Efficient Multimodal Representations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> that, though the Gemma 4 vision encoder is quite strong by itself, training the vision encoder greatly improves performance of the resulting embeddings on multimodal tasks. Analogous gains are likely possible by further training the audio encoder. Note that both runs here start with a text pre-finetuning checkpoint and run multimodal pre-finetuning, to ensure the vision encoder has not already been updated prior to either experiment.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Some MLLMs manage to additionally keep the backbone frozen <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib52" title="" class="ltx_ref">52</a>]</cite>. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hönicke et al. [49]</a></cite> similarly joins a backbone text embedding model with modality encoders, keeping each of them frozen. This prevents users from having to backfill embedding databases created with the text embedding model; however, it is possible to translate embeddings from one model’s space to another <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">53</a>]</cite>, even without access to paired data or to the original models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib54" title="" class="ltx_ref">54</a>]</cite>. Moreover, freezing a text-only backbone empirically seems to limit its ability to understand multimodal inputs, and indeed many of the strongest multimodal embedding models finetune the backbone alongside the modality encoders <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>, <a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">

</table>
</span></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S3.T5.6" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 5</span>: </span><span id="S3.T5.7" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Results with different vision token budgets (max soft tokens per image or video frame) at train and inference time. Evaluation uses a single budget for all tasks. <span id="S3.T5.7.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Top:</span> Inference-time scaling of a model trained with 280 tokens per image and 140 per video frame. <span id="S3.T5.7.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Bottom:</span> Train-time scaling with 70 vs. 140 tokens per video frame. The two experiments use different intermediate recipes.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S3.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We train EmbeddingGemma 2 with a budget of 280 vision tokens for images and 140 tokens per frame for videos, but the underlying Gemma 4 vision encoder supports budgets from 70 to 1120 tokens. In <a href="#S3.T5" title="In 3.4 Vision Token Budgets ‣ 3 Ablation Studies ‣ EmbeddingGemma 2: Unified and Efficient Multimodal Representations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> (top), we show the effect of using different vision token budgets at inference time using an intermediate checkpoint trained with 280 tokens per image and 140 per frame. Overall performance scales monotonically, with some distinct modality-specific behaviors. Visual document tasks are highly sensitive to fine-grained details and continue to improve greatly past the training budget; image quality in aggregate begins to saturate at the 280-token budget (despite continued gains on several individual tasks); and video performance actually degrades between 280 tokens and 560, likely because the excessive sequence lengths dilute attention and mean-pooled representations.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Additionally, we compare models trained with 70 vs. 140 per-frame video tokens (<a href="#S3.T5" title="In 3.4 Vision Token Budgets ‣ 3 Ablation Studies ‣ EmbeddingGemma 2: Unified and Efficient Multimodal Representations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>, bottom) to see whether training with a smaller vision budget could improve quality when using smaller vision budgets at inference time, for resource-constrained deployment. When evaluated with 70 tokens, training with 70 video tokens improves performance on video tasks, as the model is directly exposed to 70-token frames during training. But this advantage does not hold for image or visual document tasks, which drop in quality. This is likely because a) single-image tasks, which continue to be trained with 280 tokens, are treated as a separate modality and do not benefit from seeing 70-token video frames; and b) coarser video representations discard spatial details that otherwise transfer to stronger general visual representations. The latter is further supported when evaluating with 140 tokens, where training with 70 video tokens degrades performance even more, and across modalities—this makes the 140-token video budget preferable across both evaluation regimes. More gains are likely possible by increasing train-time budgets, but with seemingly diminishing returns and at a significant computational cost.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Evaluation</h2>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate EmbeddingGemma 2 on a comprehensive set of benchmarks across diverse modalities, task types, domains, and languages. Specifically, we report numbers from the Massive Text Embedding Benchmark <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">55</a>, <a href="#bib.bib56" title="" class="ltx_ref">56</a>, MTEB,]</cite> for natural language and code; the Massive Multimodal Embedding Benchmark v2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib57" title="" class="ltx_ref">57</a>, MMEB-v2,]</cite> and Massive Image Embedding Benchmark <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib58" title="" class="ltx_ref">58</a>, MIEB-lite,]</cite> for image, video, and visual documents; and the Massive Sound Embedding Benchmark and Massive Audio Embedding Benchmark for speech, music, and environmental sounds <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib59" title="" class="ltx_ref">59</a>, <a href="#bib.bib60" title="" class="ltx_ref">60</a>, MSEB and MAEB,]</cite>. We provide a summary of our results in <a href="#S4.T6" title="In 4 Evaluation ‣ EmbeddingGemma 2: Unified and Efficient Multimodal Representations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> and dive into each benchmark in more detail below.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.T6" class="ltx_table">
<div id="S4.T6.3" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_center ltx_transformed_outer" style="width:327.8pt;height:119.6pt;vertical-align:-58.4pt;"><span class="ltx_transformed_inner" style="transform:translate(-136.8pt,49.9pt) scale(0.545069600981845,0.545069600981845) ;">

<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Methods</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We select as baselines the top-ranked models on each benchmark, including both modality specialists and general-purpose embedding models which support all evaluated modalities. For MTEB, MAEB, and MIEB(lite), we compare against models under 1B parameters; for MMEB-v2, we include models under 2B parameters, as small models are scarce. Because it is one of the most directly comparable models, we evaluate <span id="S4.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">jina-embeddings-v5-omni-nano</span> on MMEB-v2 using its official implementation and verify that, on the subset reported in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hönicke et al. [49]</a></cite>, our reproduced score is slightly higher. All other baseline scores are sourced from public leaderboards. We restrict our analysis to single-vector models, given the disparity in storage and latency costs with multi-vector models, and omit models trained on <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="&gt;" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>&gt;</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">&gt;</annotation></semantics></math>25% of the evaluation data, as data contamination undermines the evaluation’s validity.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate EmbeddingGemma 2 using half-precision weights (bfloat16) and the seven types of task instructions detailed in <a href="#A1" title="Appendix A Task Instructions ‣ EmbeddingGemma 2: Unified and Efficient Multimodal Representations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Appendix</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a>. We use different sequence lengths depending on the modality and task type. For visual inputs, we use up to <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N_{\text{frm}}=32" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mtext>frm</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>32</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N_{\text{frm}}=32</annotation></semantics></math> frames per video at 140 vision tokens per frame and 280 vision tokens per image to reflect realistic model use, though we note that higher vision token budgets could yield further gains, particularly for visual documents (<a href="#S3.T5" title="In 3.4 Vision Token Budgets ‣ 3 Ablation Studies ‣ EmbeddingGemma 2: Unified and Efficient Multimodal Representations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>). Because most baseline models support limited modalities, we count only the parameters EmbeddingGemma 2 utilized for each benchmark; other models’ parameter counts are as reported on respective leaderboards.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Text</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The MTEB suite consists of a massive collection of individual, quality-controlled evaluation tasks. Together, the 162 tasks cover 250+ natural languages and 14+ programming languages, 20 domains (e.g. legal, medical, news, programming, web), and 10 task types: bitext mining, classification, clustering, instruction retrieval, multilabel classification, pair classification, reranking, retrieval, semantic text similarity (STS), and summarization.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Despite having fewer text parameters and sharing its representation space with vision and audio, EmbeddingGemma 2 improves over its predecessor on multilingual text (driven by gains in bitext mining and classification). On English, the model sees a modest regression. Only two smaller models surpass it on multilingual text, and one on English, but they are all trained as specialist text models (<a href="#A2" title="Appendix B Multilingual and English Leaderboards ‣ EmbeddingGemma 2: Unified and Efficient Multimodal Representations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Appendix</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B</span></a>). The model presents competitive text scores which outperform much larger models.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">On code (<a href="#S4.T7" title="In 4.2 Text ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ EmbeddingGemma 2: Unified and Efficient Multimodal Representations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>), EmbeddingGemma 2’s performance is stellar, establishing a new Pareto frontier. It outperforms every sub-4B model on the leaderboard and even comes within 2 points of the 28<math id="S4.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> larger frontrunner. In all three benchmarks, the model’s truncated representations degrade minimally, especially down to 256 dimensions.</p>
</div>

</section>
<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.3 </span>Vision</h3>

<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">MMEB-v2 spans 78 tasks across image, video, and visual document modalities, the latter of which includes PDFs, slides, and charts. These include retrieval, classification, question answering, visual grounding, and moment retrieval. MIEB(lite) complements this with linear-probe classification, clustering, multiple choice, compositionality, and visual semantic text similarity. They both implicitly evaluate countless visual skills like object detection, counting, optical character recognition, and temporal reasoning. They also cover various permutations of cross-modal and mixed-modal situations.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">EmbeddingGemma 2 is the smallest model on the MMEB-v2 leaderboard (<a href="#S4.T8" title="In 4.4 Audio ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ EmbeddingGemma 2: Unified and Efficient Multimodal Representations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a>). It excels especially at classification and retrieval, but provides strong scores across the board—its overall score is exceeded only by models around 2B parameters. It also outperforms various recent models including vision-language specialists with more than 8B parameters. On MIEB(lite), only two models beat EmbeddingGemma 2, and they have well over 4B parameters. Compared to top models under 1B parameters (<a href="#S4.T9" title="In 4.4 Audio ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ EmbeddingGemma 2: Unified and Efficient Multimodal Representations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a>), EmbeddingGemma 2 sets the state of the art on both aggregate metrics by a wide margin (+7.9 Task, +12.2 Type). It also offers remarkable improvements in nearly all task types, notably multilingual visual STS (+22.8) and multilingual retrieval (+12.5). Even at 128 dimensions, the model outperforms every other sub-1B model at full dimensionality.</p>
</div>
</section>

</table>
</span></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S4.T10.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 10</span>: </span><span id="S4.T10.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Performance of top-ranking models under 1B parameters on MAEB.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">MAEB includes 30 tasks encompassing five acoustic domains: speech, music, environmental, bioacoustics, and emotion. These are spread across unimodal and cross-modal tasks within retrieval, reranking, clustering, and multiple types of classification. MSEB(Retrieval) contributes a focus on multilingual speech understanding. It evaluates the model’s ability to retrieve a text passage from a spoken query, both in the same language and across languages, with a total of 26 languages and regional locales.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">On MAEB, EmbeddingGemma 2 again sets a new frontier for efficiency. Notably, among sub-1B models, it achieves state-of-the-art scores on any-to-any retrieval and audio classification (<a href="#S4.T10" title="In 4.4 Audio ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ EmbeddingGemma 2: Unified and Efficient Multimodal Representations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a>), as well as on about a third of all individual tasks. It is also state-of-the-art among models of all sizes for classification of audio pairs and a sixth of all individual tasks. Its mean task score is only about 0.2 points away from the best model under 1B parameters, and about 3.5 points away from the highest-scoring model overall. Even its 128-dimensional embeddings beat every other sub-1B model.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p3.1" class="ltx_p">On average, the model surpasses various audio-text specialists, but there is an interesting specialization divide between them. While EmbeddingGemma 2 does beat specialists like CLAP at non-speech tasks like clustering vehicle sounds (<span id="S4.SS4.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">VehicleSoundClustering</span>), these models still outperform in tasks like audio captioning (<span id="S4.SS4.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ClothoT2ARetrieval</span>). In speech tasks, EmbeddingGemma 2 sets the state of the art even in tasks with multiple languages (<span id="S4.SS4.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">FleursT2ARetrieval</span>) and singing (<span id="S4.SS4.p3.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">JamAltLyricA2TRetrieval</span>). But it sometimes struggles at zero-shot tasks with a paralinguistic focus, despite understanding the acoustics deep down. For example, it struggles tremendously at clustering speakers by gender (<span id="S4.SS4.p3.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">VoxPopuliGenderClustering</span>: 0.40), but recovers quickly when doing the same task with a linear probe (<span id="S4.SS4.p3.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">IEMOCAPGender</span>: 66.40). This indicates the model’s speech representations are dominated by semantics, desirably avoiding biases such as speaker demographic while retaining paralinguistic and acoustic attributes for extraction when needed.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p4.1" class="ltx_p">The model’s excellence on spoken language is further underscored on MSEB. Even when using ASR and text embeddings, EmbeddingGemma 2 greatly outperforms EmbeddingGemma 1, indicating the strength persists throughout modalities (<a href="#S4.T11" title="In 4.4 Audio ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ EmbeddingGemma 2: Unified and Efficient Multimodal Representations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a>). Encoding audio natively yields another even larger improvement. Instead of suffering from transcription errors from accents, homophones, or artifacts, native audio inputs preserve these signals and let the model take them into account. As a result, even the 256-dimensional embeddings greatly outperform the full-dimension ASR embeddings.</p>
</div>

</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Future Work</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our work points to several concrete directions for future research. EmbeddingGemma 2 supports long sequences and variable vision token budgets, but further extending context length, for example via content-aware methods, could enable direct indexing of full-length media, improve performance on long-horizon tasks, and support novel agentic memory systems. Innovations such as encoder-free architectures could enable both quality improvements and further reductions in memory footprint and latency. Changes in training paradigms like the introduction of end-to-end RAG training present another opportunity to further optimize embedding models for downstream use. As interleaved all-to-all multimodal search becomes more prevalent, evaluation frameworks that represent novel use cases will become more important.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">At the same time, EmbeddingGemma 2’s utility extends far beyond single-vector retrieval, serving as a general-purpose multimodal encoder. Operating on its final embeddings or unpooled token representations, the model can be adapted into (or may even excel zero-shot as) a general decision model <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib61" title="" class="ltx_ref">61</a>, <a href="#bib.bib62" title="" class="ltx_ref">62</a>, <a href="#bib.bib63" title="" class="ltx_ref">63</a>, <a href="#bib.bib64" title="" class="ltx_ref">64</a>]</cite>, model router <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib65" title="" class="ltx_ref">65</a>]</cite>, reward model <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib66" title="" class="ltx_ref">66</a>]</cite>, reranker <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib67" title="" class="ltx_ref">67</a>]</cite>, speech-to-text model <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib68" title="" class="ltx_ref">68</a>, <a href="#bib.bib69" title="" class="ltx_ref">69</a>]</cite>, late interaction retriever <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib70" title="" class="ltx_ref">70</a>, <a href="#bib.bib71" title="" class="ltx_ref">71</a>, <a href="#bib.bib72" title="" class="ltx_ref">72</a>]</cite>, and much more.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>Conclusion</h2>

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">EmbeddingGemma 2 builds on its predecessor with a smaller, stronger backbone and native multimodal capabilities. Our approach introduces improvements like simplified per-layer embeddings and a multi-stage curriculum with both modality and objective progression. This enables EmbeddingGemma 2 to set a new Pareto frontier across text, vision, and audio benchmarks, often surpassing specialist and general-purpose models several times larger. With native support for weight quantization, embedding truncation, and modular encoder loading, EmbeddingGemma 2 makes high-quality multimodal embeddings practical in resource-constrained and on-device settings. We release EmbeddingGemma 2 checkpoints to the community to accelerate research and development, for both off-the-shelf use and as a foundational multimodal encoder.</p>
</div>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
</section>

    <p>We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile
      support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the
      methods listed below:</p>
    <ul>
      <li>Click the "Report Issue" <span class="mobile-only">(<svg role="presentation"
            style="display: inline-block; vertical-align: middle; fill: var(--text-color);" aria-hidden="true"
            height="1em" viewBox="0 0 640 640">
            <path
              d="M224 160C224 107 267 64 320 64C373 64 416 107 416 160L416 163.6C416 179.3 403.3 192 387.6 192L252.5 192C236.8 192 224.1 179.3 224.1 163.6L224.1 160zM569.6 172.8C580.2 186.9 577.3 207 563.2 217.6L465.4 290.9C470.7 299.8 474.7 309.6 477.2 320L576 320C593.7 320 608 334.3 608 352C608 369.7 593.7 384 576 384L480 384L480 416C480 418.6 479.9 421.3 479.8 423.9L563.2 486.4C577.3 497 580.2 517.1 569.6 531.2C559 545.3 538.9 548.2 524.8 537.6L461.7 490.3C438.5 534.5 395.2 566.5 344 574.2L344 344C344 330.7 333.3 320 320 320C306.7 320 296 330.7 296 344L296 574.2C244.8 566.5 201.5 534.5 178.3 490.3L115.2 537.6C101.1 548.2 81 545.3 70.4 531.2C59.8 517.1 62.7 497 76.8 486.4L160.2 423.9C160.1 421.3 160 418.7 160 416L160 384L64 384C46.3 384 32 369.7 32 352C32 334.3 46.3 320 64 320L162.8 320C165.3 309.6 169.3 299.8 174.6 290.9L76.8 217.6C62.7 207 59.8 186.9 70.4 172.8C81 158.7 101.1 155.8 115.2 166.4L224 248C236.3 242.9 249.8 240 264 240L376 240C390.2 240 403.7 242.8 416 248L524.8 166.4C538.9 155.8 559 158.7 569.6 172.8z" />
          </svg>)</span> button, located in the page header.</li>
    </ul>
    <p><strong>Tip:</strong> You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.</p>
    <p>Our team has already identified <a class="ltx_ref" href="https://github.com/arXiv/html_feedback/issues"
        target="_blank">the following issues</a>. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we
      may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability
      should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for
      all.</p>
    <p>Have a free development cycle? Help support accessibility at arXiv! Our collaborators at LaTeXML maintain a <a
        class="ltx_ref" href="https://github.com/brucemiller/LaTeXML/wiki/Porting-LaTeX-packages-for-LaTeXML"
        target="_blank">list of packages that need conversion</a>, and welcome <a class="ltx_ref"
        href="https://github.com/brucemiller/LaTeXML/issues" target="_blank">developer contributions</a>.</p>
  </div>
